preamble: The shift from the voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] to the voiceless glottal fricative [h] is a debuccalization: the labial constriction is lost and friction remains only at the glottis. The textbook case is Japanese, where Old Japanese *p became [ɸ] in Middle Japanese (written ⟨f⟩ in Portuguese missionary works and ⟨ph⟩/⟨hw⟩ in the Korean textbook Ch'ŏphae Sinŏ) and then [h] in Early Modern Japanese, except before /u/, where [ɸ] survives. Synchronic [ɸ] ~ [h] variation is documented for Māori ⟨wh⟩, and a bilabial [ɸ] stage is widely reconstructed (though not directly attested) for the Old Castilian change of Latin f- to h-. Because [ɸ] is itself a cross-linguistically uncommon phoneme, the change is attested in only a handful of well-described cases; commonality is set to 3.

examples.note: 'mother'; the attested chain is /papa/ > /ɸaɸa/ > /ɸawa/ > /ɸaɸa/ > /haha/ (Wiktionary, citing Nihon Kokugo Daijiten)
The shift to [h] did not apply before /u/, so modern /h/ is still realized [ɸ] in that position

In recordings of a speaker born in 1885, [ɸ] was the most frequent realization of wh, but whaka- was realized with [h] (plus a rounded vowel) in 22 of 34 tokens; [h] appears almost exclusively before /a/ (Maclagan and King 2002)

examples.from: Latin facere 'to do' > Old Spanish fazer
examples.note: Reconstructed chain [f] > [ɸ] > [h] > ∅ (Penny); the [ɸ] stage is inferred, not directly attested
Initial [h] from Latin f- survives in rural western dialects (e.g. Extremadura, western Andalusia).
